units.text: A violin cannot produce every imaginable sound through any gesture. A sculptural bridge must bear its own weight. A painter works with light, pigments, surfaces and a visual system. Art is not a territory outside nature. But these constraints do not yield a single legitimate style or an eternal canon of beauty.

Three levels must be separated here: physical possibility, perceptual effect and cultural value. Physics can help us understand sound production. Psychology can investigate what particular people distinguish or prefer under particular conditions. Art criticism and history discuss meaning and value in context. No level can automatically replace another.

A numerical ratio between frequencies is a measurable property. The claim that the ratio suits every music, listener and purpose is much stronger. Even if we found a robust perceptual preference, it would not follow that art ought to maximize it. The artist may pursue unease, ambiguity, tension or surprise, not merely comfort.

The same happens with visual symmetry. It can be an organizing tool. Asymmetry can express movement or conflict. Our ability to recognize a pattern does not oblige every work to reproduce it. A constraint is a condition of the game; an aesthetic norm is a choice about how it is worth playing.

Claims about universal proportions supposedly explaining beauty on their own also deserve caution. Retrospectively finding a ratio in a sufficiently complex object is easy if we can freely choose measurement points. A test would require measurements fixed beforehand, comparisons with alternatives and an effect criterion. Without these, mathematics can ornament an impression rather than explain it.

The concept of law also influences art through order’s prestige. An artist may seek the world’s essence in geometric forms, repetition or rule variations. Another may think precisely the rule’s rupture makes experience visible. We need not choose either intention as nature’s truth. We can judge what the work accomplishes and what question it forces us to formulate.

Generative art offers an especially clear conceptual laboratory. We fix a few rules and obtain a family of results. From this family we select some works. What part of the value comes from the rule, what part from the initial state and what part from selection? If we show only successful results, the audience may attribute to the algorithm a power the complete process does not possess to the same extent.

This is not an accusation against algorithmic generation. Artists working manually also select, revise and abandon. The question is what we present as the creative mechanism. ‘A simple rule produced this image’ can be true and incomplete if thousands of failed attempts preceded the choice. The full explanation also includes the filter.

This observation returns us to emergence. A complex form may arise from simple rules, but not every complexity is meaningful to an observer. Meaning may depend on experience, conventions and intentions. Explaining the pixel distribution does not mean explaining why someone sees loss or promise in it.

Who benefits when an aesthetic norm is called ‘natural’? Those who master it and institutions using it as a filter may gain legitimacy. Who loses? Forms of expression evaluated by a criterion concealing its contextual character. But pluralism does not require asserting every object is equally well made either. We can assess coherence, difficulty, precision and effect without pretending our preference is written in the atom’s structure.

Perhaps the most interesting link between art and laws of nature is not that art illustrates them. It is that art teaches us to notice how many worlds of meaning can be built without changing basic constraints. The same sounds can belong to different songs. The same materials can become shelter or monument. Freedom does not necessarily begin where rules disappear; sometimes it begins where we understand what a rule permits without commanding.
